definition: The four NTFS timestamps — Modified, Accessed, Changed, Born — stored twice per file, once in $STANDARD_INFORMATION and once in $FILE_NAME, on different update rules.
The NTFS attribute (type 0x10) holding the MACB timestamps most tools display by default — easy for a user-mode tool to modify, which is why it's the usual timestomping target.
The NTFS attribute (type 0x10) holding a second, independent MACB timestamp set, updated far more restrictively by the OS — the harder-to-reach control group for detecting timestomping.
Deliberately altering a file's timestamps to hide its true creation or modification time, usually to blend malicious activity into a legitimate-looking timeline.
The principle that evidence should be collected starting with what disappears fastest — CPU registers and RAM before disk, disk before backups.

Documentation proving who handled a piece of evidence, when, and what they did to it — in enterprise IR, scoped to what's actually needed for internal and regulatory accountability, not criminal-prosecution admissibility.
A forensic artifact — a hash, IP, domain, file path, or registry key — indicating a system may be compromised by a specific threat.
Attacker behavior described at three levels of specificity: the high-level goal, the general method, and the exact implementation.
A vendor-neutral, publicly maintained framework cataloging attacker tactics and techniques — the shared vocabulary this academy's artifact pages map back to.
A model ranking indicator types by how costly they are for an attacker to change — hashes are cheap to burn, TTPs are expensive, which is where detection investment pays off most.
An intrusion-analysis model built around four vertices — adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim — used to pivot between related indicators during an investigation.
A long-lived credential issued at sign-in that silently renews short-lived access tokens in the background — not invalidated by a later password change unless explicitly revoked.
The Microsoft Graph PowerShell cmdlet that forcibly invalidates a user's refresh tokens, ending active sessions across every device and application at once.
A hybrid identity sync method where a hash of the on-premises AD password hash is synced to Entra ID, which then authenticates independently using that synced hash.
A hybrid identity method where Entra ID validates each sign-in against on-premises AD directly via an agent, rather than syncing a password hash.
A hybrid identity method where authentication is delegated entirely to an on-premises federation server; Entra ID never sees or stores password material.
A technique abusing legitimate AD replication permissions to request password hashes for any account, including krbtgt, without direct access to a real domain controller's files.
A forged Kerberos TGT built from a stolen krbtgt hash, granting domain-wide access that bypasses normal authentication until krbtgt is properly reset.
Requesting a service ticket for any account with a registered SPN, then attempting to crack the ticket offline — requires no elevated privilege to begin.
NTFS's append-only change journal, recording file-system events independently of the $MFT — a corroborating source that survives even when the $MFT record it describes has been altered.
A Windows performance feature that incidentally leaves forensic evidence of program execution, including run count and files/DLLs touched on first launch.
A registry-backed cache of file metadata used for application-compatibility checks — evidence of file presence, not reliably evidence of execution.
The Windows process that holds credential material in memory for active sessions — a primary credential-theft target and a key artifact in memory forensics.
A DNS-published list of servers authorized to send mail for a domain, checked against the message's envelope sender — not the visible From header.
A cryptographic signature proving a message's signed content wasn't altered in transit — says nothing on its own about who the envelope sender was.
A policy requiring SPF or DKIM to align with the visible From domain, and telling receivers what to do when they don't — explicitly does not cover display-name spoofing.
Router/switch-generated connection metadata — who talked to whom, how much, for how long — without packet content, cheap enough to retain far longer than full packet capture.
